prize_parts.citation: for the experimental realisation of Hubbard models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition to fermionic and single-site-resolved quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter

statement.case_for: I keep B020 with Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger as my final position. After the full exchange my reasoning is unchanged in substance and somewhat firmer in its framing. The discovery I would reward is that model Hamiltonians for strongly correlated matter, the Bose- and Fermi-Hubbard models, can be realised as tunable, isolated, directly imaged laboratory systems. The superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition, the fermionic Hubbard work and the quantum-gas microscope each opened a regime in which correlations are read out atom by atom, and theory and experiment agree quantitatively. Two decades of reproduction in many laboratories answers my usual question about robustness. The chair's question asks whether the discovery is the proposal plus the Mott observation or the experimental realisation including fermions and single sites. I take the second. The prize is for a body of experimental demonstrations that made a simulator of correlated electrons possible, and the fermionic and microscopy steps are what connect it to the correlated-electron problem. Lindroth and Kroll both regard B020 as mature, and the committee has now shown it is the one candidate on which colleagues from different subfields converge, which counts as scientific evidence of robustness and not just a head count.
statement.case_against: The credit remains the weakest part. Any three of the five supplied names leave out someone with a real claim: Zoller and Jaksch for the proposal, Cirac for the theory around it, and Hansch for the early lattice work. The experimental trio reads as incomplete to anyone who counts the proposal as the discovery. The doped Hubbard model and the pseudogap, which would be the decisive payoff, are still unsolved, so critics (Eriksson, Olsson, Mehlig and Kroll) can fairly say that the platform is mature while its headline result is not. BEC (2001) and ion and photon control (2012) are also close in prize history, and I am not the best judge of how much novelty that removes. B024 is cleaner on attribution and confirmation than my choice and I would not call it an inferior alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth answers the maturity worry by saying the Mott transition and single-site observation were themselves the discovery, and she keeps Zoller in the trio to credit the Jaksch-Zoller proposal.
responses.response: I accept her argument that the Mott transition and single-site resolution are results and not a promise, and that settles the maturity question for me. Where we still differ is the third name. The proposal is important, but Zoller also stands in B006, and with Cirac that makes the theory credit for lattices and ions overlap in a way the committee would have to explain. Dropping Esslinger leaves fermionic Hubbard physics without an experimental voice, and that is the part closest to correlated electrons. If she can show that the Zoller name is needed to define the discovery and not to honour the proposal, I would reconsider. As it stands I keep Esslinger, and I will rank her trio as the nearest variant of my own.

responses.point: Kroll holds B024 first because lattice clocks are the cleanest reproduced measurement, while conceding that the payoff so far is mostly tighter limits, proximity to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and a redefinition of the second that has not happened.
responses.response: I agree that clocks are the best confirmed result on the shortlist and I keep B024 as my first alternative. The chair asked him whether magic-wavelength lattices and 10^-18 differ enough from the earlier prizes. I think they do in method, but his own reservation, that the output so far is better limits and not a new fact about nature, is the reason I put B020 ahead. The lattice simulators produced states that had not been prepared before, and the clocks perfected a known quantity. I cannot judge priority in metrology and defer to him, but the pending redefinition of the second suggests that the clock case may be stronger in a few years than it is now, so a later B024 prize loses less than a later B020 prize does.

responses.point: Mehlig and Eriksson hold B021 because a clean prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald) was followed by observation in 2018, and they regard the unsettled pairing mechanism as a follow-up question.
responses.response: I find the prediction-then-observation chain compelling and I can follow the broad replication in moire systems. My hesitation is the chair's question about pairing: Mehlig himself says he cares whether a breakthrough is understood, and the superconducting phase, which is half the headline, is not understood yet. Twist-angle disorder also makes sample details hard to reproduce. I accept that this is a judgement call and defer to the condensed-matter members on how much it matters. If the committee prefers a young, strongly replicated field, B021 is a respectable choice, but I would then ask for the two-name or the three-name decision to be made on whether Bistritzer's contribution is the prediction itself, which I cannot judge.

responses.point: Pearce proposes a two-part prize, B052 (Halzen alone) plus B024 (Katori, Ye), and names the one-name IceCube credit as the weakest point.
responses.response: I agree with his own diagnosis of the weak point. A one-name prize for a collaboration of this size would be hard to defend, and the two parts share no theme, so I would not support the pairing as it stands. I am outside my field on neutrino astronomy and defer to him and Danielsson on the science. His point that the instrument-building criterion applies to quantum-gas microscopy as well as to IceCube remains, in my view, a reason to treat B020 as a serious candidate for those who favour detector-driven discovery. I would support B024 as a single part before the combined configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson puts B021 first and lists B024 and B020 as alternatives, noting that lattice quantum simulation and clocks have two decades of confirmation while moire physics is eight years old.
responses.response: I appreciate that he treats B020 as a credible second choice on maturity grounds, and he is right that age is the main difference between our lists. I share his hesitation that the doped Hubbard question is open, and I do not think a committee should pretend otherwise. But I read the established, quantitative results as sufficient, and my reading of the chair's question is that the pairing question in B021 is a larger gap than the doped-Hubbard gap in B020, because the latter is a goal and the former is part of the claimed discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts an experimental trio for B020, or considers the Jaksch-Zoller proposal part of the discovery and so wants Zoller named, with the overlap with B006 that this brings.
Whether Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger fairly represent the Mott-insulator, fermionic Hubbard and microscopy results, given that Hansch, Jaksch and Cirac are outside the credited trio.
Whether the doped Hubbard question is a pending payoff that a prize can safely precede, or a sign that a decisive result is still ahead.
Whether B024 would be the safer choice if the committee wants a sharply bounded, fully confirmed result, which I cannot judge from priority history.
statement.conflict_note: I am a theorist in superconducting circuits and director of WACQT at Chalmers, and I know the people in the circuit-QED candidate B002 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin), so I would recuse myself from any final decision on B002 and be cautious about B026 and B022. B002 is no longer my preferred configuration. My profile shows no personal, institutional or funding connection to B020, B024 or B006 or their credited names; WACQT has only an indirect cold-atom link through Lund and KTH collaborators who are not among the credited names.
